passage.text: There was no positive ill-nature in Maria or Julia; and though Fanny was often mortified by their treatment of her, she thought too lowly of her own claims to feel injured by it. His eldest son was careless and extravagant, and had already given him much uneasiness; but his other children promised him nothing but good. Once, and once only, in the course of many years, had she the happiness of being with William. Edmund's friendship never failed her: his leaving Eton for Oxford made no change in his kind dispositions, and only afforded more frequent opportunities of proving them. Kept back as she was by everybody else, his single support could not bring her forward; but his attentions were otherwise of the highest importance in assisting the improvement of her mind, and extending its pleasures. He knew her to be clever, to have a quick apprehension as well as good sense, and a fondness for reading, which, properly directed, must be an education in itself. In return for such services she loved him better than anybody in the world except William: her heart was divided between the two.
